full_judgment:
2. Respondents have filed an affidavit in opposition and in paragraph 4 it is stated that he was arrested along with certain central leaders of Jatiyo Samajtantric Dal when the residence of the Minister was gheraoed at Dacca. He was released on 20-6-75 on execution of a bond. In paragraph 5 it is stated that the detenu visited Rajshahi in June and July 1575 as he was deputed by the party leaders to organise the party and the underground armed cadre for which he contacted leading workers of Jatiyo Samajtantrick Dal (Rab-Siraj Group). It is stated that he was arrested on 4-8-76 en 20-30 hours under rule 30 of the Emergency Powers Rules when he was returning back from the house of one of the underground leaders of Chhatra League. Subsequently on 11.8.76 the detention order under rule 5(1)(a) was passed. It is denied that he was tortured by the police. In paragraph 7 it is reiteratcd that the detenu was an accused in Ramna P. S. Case No. 167 (3) 74 in connection with gherao of the residence of a Minister. It is further stated that materials would be placed before the court at the time of hearing. 

 (i) Period between 17.3.74 to 20.6.75. During this period detenu was in jail in connection with Ramna P. S. Case No. 167 (3) 74 for allegedly gheraoing the house of a Minister. 

 7. In criminal Misc. case No. 34 of 1976 we had considered a similar argument and we had quoted the observation of Hedayetulla, J. of Indian Supreme Court which was also followed with approval in the case of Pushkar Mukherjee Vs. State reported in A.I.R. 1970 (S.C.) 852 that "by using the expression" maintenance of law and order" the District Magistrate was widening his oven field of action and was adding a clause to the Defence of India Rules.". In that view of the matter the detention was found to be illegal. 

 8. In the case of Eripa Sindbu Hajra Vs. State in Criminal Misc. case No. 69 of 1977 this Court has held amongst others that emergency is a circumstance which has to be considered as a factor while considering the validity of the order of detention but when that detention is challenged the onus under section 106 of the Evidence Act is on the respondents to show that they had materials against the detenu which necessitated the order of detention. Applying that principle in the facts and circumstances of the case we are constrained to mention that the detaining authority has not placed any material before this court which would lend justification for detaining the detenu on the ground that he should be detained so that he cannot act prejudicially to the security, public safety or interest of Bangladesh. As has been mentioned above the learned Advocate for the petitioner had admirably broken the period in question and argued that from 17-3-74 to 20-6-75 the detenu was in jail. So, there cannot be any question of his prejudicial activity. Next, from 20-6-75 to 15-8-75 no material has been placed as to give the impression that the detenu was carrying out any prejudicial activity. From 16-8-75 to 30-7-76 there is no report from any quarter of the law enforcing agency that the detenu was acting in any manner which calls for his preventive detention. We have gone through the entire file and save and except the fact that the detenu was arrested at about 8-30 P.M. on 4-8-76 and then on interrogation he gave out that he came to Rajshahi for organising the students as per direction of his party, there is nothing else on the file. Moreover, there is no report by the law-enforcing agency that the detenu was activizing the armed cadres or organising them excepting a report which filed on 6-8-76 after the arrest. The statement of the detenu itself does not reveal that he was given any task of activizing any arm cadre except to organise student front. 

 9. The argument has force. The materials disclose that he came to Rajshahi on 30-7-76. The detenu's version is that he came to prosecute his further studies in another subjects and the version of the respondents is that he had come to organise the underground armed cadres for which there is no material on the record. It was stated in the affidavit in opposition that the materials would be placed before this court at the time of hearing "as the same are secret in nature." We have gone through all the materials and we are constrained to mention that not a single report discloses the fact that he was organising the armed miscreants group prior to 5-8-76. As a matter of fact, all the reports are filed after 5-8-76, in other words, after his arrest and not before his arrest. Therefore, the apprehension of the detaining authority was grounded on which material becomes important. The preventive detention is called for only when certain prejudicial activity creates impression in the mind of the detaining authority, if the subject is allowed to remain free then he is likely to act prejudicially endangering the security, interest of Bangladesh or safety etc. This apprehension can be formed, has there been antecedent or history sheet of the detenu. There is none excepting that he took part in Farakka missil under the leardership of Moulana Bhashani which by no means can be termed as prejudicial activity. The fact that he took part in gherao movement of the house of a Minister is a single act for which specific criminal charge has been levelled against him. Apart from that incident there is nothing. The respondents have not placed before us any other materials to show that antecedent of the detenu is such that his behaviour pattern would allow him to indulge in prejudicial activities. The fact that he was a general Secretary of Chhatra. League in his student days could not by itself show that he is the person who answered the description of the people who are to be taken in under the law of preventing detention, namely Emergency Powers Rules. In other words, the potentiality of this detenu to act prejudicially has not been satisfactorily established on materials and no reasonable person could come to this conclusion that if he is allowed to remain at large he would indulge in such activities. The next is the satisfaction as required by rule 5(l)(a) is a onerous responsibility which must be found on concrete materials. Now it is well settled that such law is to be viewed with scrutinising eye so that the liberty is not put into jeopardy even at the time of emergency. As we have said emergency is no doubt a factor to weigh the activity of the detenu. Here in this case no such foundation had been laid for the exercise of passing the order of detention under the Emergency Powers Rules.
